findings.claim: should_encode duplicates the Packed-unwrapping ternary already implemented in column_subset, instead of calling a shared helper. If a second wrapper type is ever added, only one of the two call sites might get updated.
findings.source: columnstore.py:53 (`alias = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind`) duplicated at columnstore.py:63 (`kind = col.kind.primitive if isinstance(col.kind, Packed) else col.kind`)
findings.remedy: Extract a single `_unwrap_kind(kind: str | Packed) -> str` helper and call it from both `column_subset` and `should_encode`.

findings.claim: should_encode's hardcoded kind set includes 'masked_text', but no test exercises a masked_text column (plain or Packed), so a regression that silently drops it from the set would go undetected -- unlike 'text' and 'choice', which are covered.
findings.source: columnstore.py:64 (`return kind in {"text", "masked_text", "choice"}`); test_columnstore.py:17-26 `_table()` fixture defines only text/number/choice/packed_name/packed_grade columns, none with kind 'masked_text'
findings.remedy: Add a masked_text column (plain and Packed) to `_table()` and assert it's included in `encode_categoricals`.

findings.claim: _DERIVED_PATTERN's optional `Tagged[` group exists specifically to catch a Tagged-wrapped Derived marker when the whole annotation fails to resolve, but no test exercises that combination -- every Tagged test in test_fieldspec.py resolves successfully, and every unresolved-forward-ref test is a bare (non-Tagged) Derived.
findings.source: fieldspec.py:24 (`_DERIVED_PATTERN = re.compile(r"((\w+\.)?Tagged\[)?(\w+\.)?Derived\[")`); test_fieldspec.py has test_tagged_wrapped_derived_field_is_excluded (fully resolvable) and test_bare_forward_ref_derived_field_is_excluded (unresolvable, but no Tagged wrapper) -- no test combines both
findings.remedy: Add a test like `stored_field_names({'cached_total': 'Tagged[Derived[Missing], "cache"]'}, NAMESPACE)` asserting exclusion, to prove the regex fallback covers the exact case its optional Tagged group was written for.

findings.claim: The CHANGES.md limitation note is scoped only to a locally-aliased Derived import combined with an unresolvable forward reference. Tracing _resolve/_DERIVED_PATTERN shows the identical 'can't be recognized' failure also occurs for a locally-aliased Tagged import (e.g. `from tags import Tagged as T`) wrapping an unresolvable annotation, since `.match()` anchors at position 0 and an alias name won't match the pattern's literal `Tagged[`.
findings.source: fieldspec.py:24 (literal `Tagged\[` in the pattern); CHANGES.md:11-19 limitation note ('a field locally aliased to a registry's `Derived` object ... whose annotation is *also* an unresolvable forward reference')
findings.remedy: Broaden the CHANGES.md note to state the fallback is alias-sensitive for both names the pattern hardcodes (`Tagged` and `Derived`), not just `Derived`.

findings.claim: markers_legacy.py imports and reuses the underscore-prefixed _MarkerForm from markers_native, crossing a module boundary via a name whose leading underscore conventionally signals 'private to this module'.
findings.remedy: If _MarkerForm is genuinely a shared building block, drop the leading underscore (or move it to a small shared module) so the import doesn't cross a declared privacy boundary.

findings.claim: Span.__lt__ rebuilds the full ordered member list on every comparison instead of reusing the module-level SPANS list, duplicating exactly the 'copied at each call site' pattern the file's own docstring says was eliminated by this refactor.
findings.source: lifespan.py:32 (`order = list(self.__class__)`) vs lifespan.py:36 (`SPANS = list(Span)`); docstring at lifespan.py:7 ('now backed by one ordered enum instead of a mapping copied at each call site')
findings.remedy: Have `__lt__` use `SPANS.index(self) < SPANS.index(other)` (reordering the module so SPANS is defined before the class if needed), so there's one ordered list, not two.

findings.claim: Handle.span changed from a plain writable attribute to a read-only property. CHANGES.md's compatibility claim is carefully scoped to callers that only read .span, but no test verifies the write-path: a caller that used to assign .span now hits AttributeError instead of succeeding.
findings.source: lifespan.py:70-72 (`@property\n    def span(self) -> str:\n        return self._span.value` -- no setter); CHANGES.md:9-11 ('Every existing caller that only ever read `.span` sees no change')
findings.remedy: Add a test asserting `handle.span = 'x'` raises AttributeError (documenting the intentional break), and confirm no in-repo caller ever assigns `.span` directly before shipping.

findings.claim: QuietQueue is a dead, unreferenced actor declared purely for a hypothetical future concurrency plan -- it's never instantiated or wired into Workspace, child(), or main.swift.
findings.source: workspace.swift:57-59 (`// Reserved for a future default execution context; not wired into any\n// scoping path yet.\nactor QuietQueue {}`)
findings.remedy: Delete QuietQueue until an actual caller needs it; add it back, with its real usage, when the concurrency requirement is concrete.

findings.claim: test_platform_guards.py's bundled suite only calls collect_skips(MAINLAND, ALL_TESTS); it never calls collect_skips on GEARSHIFT or TIDELINE. MAINLAND is precisely the platform where is_driftplane is trivially False regardless of implementation, so the passing suite gives no evidence for CHANGES.md's actual claim -- that the three is_driftplane-guarded tests still skip identically on both sandboxed platforms after the consolidation.
findings.source: test_platform_guards.py:74-76 (`skipped = collect_skips(MAINLAND, ALL_TESTS)\n    assert skipped == {}, f"mainland should skip nothing, got {skipped}"`); CHANGES.md:11-12 ('No test's skip/run outcome changes on any platform')
findings.remedy: Add collect_skips(GEARSHIFT, ALL_TESTS) and collect_skips(TIDELINE, ALL_TESTS) assertions checking the exact skip set on each: all is_driftplane-guarded tests skip on both; single-platform guards skip only on their platform; the two combined-guard tests skip on both.

findings.claim: collect_skips iterates a test's __skip_guards__ in decorator-application order (innermost/bottom decorator first), which is the reverse of the visual top-to-bottom order the guards are written in for test_unix_socket_creation and test_bare_thread_spawn; harmless today only because each test's stacked guards target mutually exclusive platforms.
findings.source: platsupport.py:39-45 (`def decorator(func):\n        guards = list(getattr(func, "__skip_guards__", ()))\n        guards.append((predicate, reason))` -- each decorator appends, and decorators apply bottom-up); test_platform_guards.py:50-53 test_unix_socket_creation stacks `@skip_if(is_gearshift, ...)` above `@skip_if(is_tideline, ...)` in source but tideline's guard lands first in the list
findings.remedy: Note in skip_if's docstring that evaluation order follows decorator-application (bottom-up), or reverse the append so evaluation order matches source order, before anyone adds overlapping guards where order matters.
